title: Political persuasion can travel through repeated physical proximity, not only ideology or formal affiliation
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 34925; randomized U.S. Senate seating assignments, recorded interactions, and legislative votes over a 30-year sample

observations.period: Thirty-year Senate sample; paper issued March 2026

denominator.unit: years in the analyzed Senate voting sample; bill and senator denominators vary by outcome

close_peer_vote_shift.unit: percentage-point shift in Congressional voting associated with randomly assigned close peers

distance_range.unit: feet; reported range over which the closest-peer distance effect persists before dissipating

aisle_crossing.value: close peers increase voting with the opposite party; the effect is roughly eight times larger on final votes

counterfactual_bill_outcomes.unit: consequential bills estimated to have switched outcomes over the sample under randomized seating counterfactuals

observations.method: Randomized Senate seating assignments identify peer exposure; AI-enhanced computer vision of C-SPAN video records face-to-face interactions at ten-second intervals, which are linked to immediately pending votes.
observations.uncertainty: The study concerns legislators in a highly institutional setting, not voters generally. Proximity is randomized, but observed interaction mechanisms and effects may not transport to ordinary social networks, campaigns, or online platforms.
observations.subgroup: U.S. Senators, close physical peers, aisle-seated senators, party and state contexts, and final versus earlier votes.
observations.counterinterpretation: The finding does not show that proximity alone changes public opinion or that cross-party contact always moderates conflict; Senate norms, agenda selection, and strategic interaction remain relevant.

boundary: This record adds a causal micro-mechanism for political action: physical and repeated peer exposure can affect legislative voting. It does not establish a general solution to polarization, mass persuasion, public trust, or durable constituent realignment.
